name: Latvian
confidence_why: 4 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 2 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_quote: Latvian has word-initial stress. In modern, urban dialects, the word initial syllable is the only one that carries extra prominence.
sweep_summary: Three works with stress in the title for Latvian. (1) Kariņš 1996 BLS 22 'Optimal stress feet in Latvian' — downloaded open (BLS site needs a browser UA; scan scanned at 300 dpi), read: first syllable receives primary stress regardless of weight (undominated ALIGNHEAD), secondary stress via moraic trochees (short words) / syllabic trochees (long words) from Endzelins 1922 data — confirms fixed-strict and offers a secondary-stress rule. (2) Kariņš 1996 UPenn dissertation — not in the UPenn repository (three DSpace API queries, 0 hits), ProQuest/print only; medium priority, expected to restate the same analysis at length. (3) Ekblom 1933 'Die lettischen Akzentarten' — 80-page experimental-phonetic study of the three syllable intonations from Endzelins' own pronunciation (LIBRIS record; described first-hand in Kariņš 1997 p.186); prosody but not word stress; no digital copy found; low priority. Bonus: Kariņš 1997 BLS 23 'Lexical tone and stress in Latvian' (works still to obtain previously unfetched) also downloaded and read: 'Main word stress in Latvian occurs on the first syllable of a word' (p.186), tone independent of stress, and a documented non-initial-stress lexeme nekad 'never' (p.193) — refines (lexical exceptions in ne- compounds). Best new first-hand statement: Kariņš 1996 BLS p.210; it confirms but does not supersede the catalog's deciding source (Endzelin 1923 reference grammar). All downloaded files and catalogue lookups logged in

new_statements.reading: Fixed initial primary stress, weight-insensitive, with trochaic secondary stress: moraic trochees L->R in 2-3 syllable words, syllabic trochees L->R in 4-5 syllable words, plus stem-stressed morphological exceptions. Confirms the catalog's fixed-strict (initial) coding and supplies a secondary-stress rule (the secondary-stress rule) the record lacks. The companion 1997 paper (p.186 'Main word stress in Latvian occurs on the first syllable of a word'; p.193 nekad 'never' with primary stress on the second syllable) adds that a small class of ne- compounds has non-initial primary stress — a lexical exception, not a change of type.

tone_statements.citation: Derksen, Rick. 2024. The accentuation of Latvian Curonianisms. Baltistica 59(1), 57-81. doi:10.15388/baltistica.59.1.2543
tone_statements.quote: P r o n k (2017, 661) offers a phonetic explanation for the West Latvian merger of the broken tone and the falling tone … We know that the West Latvian system with two tones arose from a threefold tonal opposition. Since the Curonian system has not been recorded, it is always possible to come up with a scenario that fits the facts. Does the Selonian rising tone, which is found instead of broken tone, reflect the prosodic system of the Selonians? … What about the East Latvian merger of the sustained tone and the falling tone?
tone_statements.locator: p. 74, §3 'Language contact and Curonian'; cf. p. 73 §2.5 'sustained tone or broken tone in the Central Latvian system with three tones' and p. 58
tone_statements.summary: Three tones (sustained, falling, broken) in Central Latvian; West Latvian merges broken and falling, East Latvian merges sustained and falling; Selonian has rising for broken. Fixed initial stress.

tone_statements.citation: Švageris, Evaldas. 2021. Further investigation of the interaction of prosodic elements in the Baltic languages: a perception-based analysis of Latvian lexical tones. Baltistica 56(2), 271-305. doi:10.15388/baltistica.56.2.2435 (CC-BY; PDFhttps://www.zurnalai.vu.lt/baltistica/article/download/39271/36826)
tone_statements.quote: Viso to pasekmė – dvi norminės latvių kalbos priegaidžių sistemos: senesnioji trinarė (krintančioji, laužtinė ir tęstinė priegaidės) ir naujesnioji dvinarė (tęstinė ir netęstinė priegaidės; žr. M a r k u s, B o n d 2010, 53–54; LVG 2013, 105; H u a l d e, R i a d 2018). Glotalizacija veikiau laikytina ryškiu netęstinės (laužtinės) priegaidės požymiu, tačiau, atsižvelgiant į šių dienų prozodines realijas, niekaip negalinčiu pretenduoti į invariantyvaus rodiklio statusą.
tone_statements.translation: The consequence of all this is two normative Latvian tone systems: the older three-member one (falling, broken and level tones) and the newer two-member one (level and non-level tones; see Markus & Bond 2010, 53-54; LVG 2013, 105; Hualde & Riad 2018). Glottalization is rather to be regarded as a salient feature of the non-level (broken) tone, but, given present-day prosodic realities, one that can in no way claim the status of an invariant indicator.
tone_statements.locator: p. 282 (section 'Tyrimo rezultatai', paragraph beginning on p. 281)
tone_statements.summary: Standard Latvian lexical tones on stressed long syllables: newer two-way system level vs non-level (broken), tested here with zãle ~ zâle; an older three-way norm (falling, broken, level) also exists.

tone_statements.citation: Švageris, Evaldas. 2020. Effect of intonation on phonetic realization of lexical tones: experimental investigation of standard Latvian [Intonacijos įtaka akustinei priegaidžių raiškai: eksperimentinis latvių bendrinės kalbos tyrimas]. Baltistica 55(1), 119-157. doi:10.15388/baltistica.55.1.2414 (CC-BY; PDFhttps://www.journals.vu.lt/baltistica/article/download/39351/36904)
tone_statements.quote: Nuoseklumo dėlei abi poros pasirinktos su laužtine ir tęstine priegaidėmis. Nors oficialioji latvių kalbos norma nurodo dvi gretutines priegaidžių sistemas (tęstinės ir netęstinės; tęstinės, laužtinės ir krintančiosios), tačiau apie trinarį priegaidžių modelį, regis, labiau kalbama iš tradicijos. Naujesni tyrimai rodo (G r i g o r j e v s, R e m e r t s 2004, 41–49; M a r k u s, B o n d 2010, 52–64; B o n d, M a r k u s, S t o c k m a l 2015, 399–410), kad daugumoje tarmių ir bendrinėje kalboje priegaidžių opoziciją sudaro du, o ne trys nariai.
tone_statements.translation: For consistency both pairs were chosen with the broken and the level (sustained) tone. Although the official norm of Latvian gives two parallel tone systems (level and non-level; level, broken and falling), the three-member tone model seems to be spoken of more out of tradition. Newer studies show (Grigorjevs & Remerts 2004; Markus & Bond 2010; Bond, Markus & Stockmal 2015) that in most dialects and in the standard language the tone opposition consists of two, not three, members.
tone_statements.summary: Two contrastive tones on stressed long vowels in standard Latvian, level (sustained) vs non-level (broken); the traditional falling tone is not distinct in the standard language and most dialects.

tone_statements.citation: Kramer [first name not on the anonymous abstract]. 2019. The hybrid pitch accent-tone-stress system of Latvian. 2-pp. abstract, poster session 2, Annual Meeting on Phonology (AMP 2019), Stony Brook University.https://www.stonybrook.edu/commcms/amp2019/_pdf/_Poster2/2.2Kramer.pdf
tone_statements.quote: Standard Latvian has a three-way pitch accent contrast, distinguishing between level, falling and broken accent (1). The latter is comparable to Danish and Lithuanian stød (e.g., Basbøll 2005, Kiparsky 2015, respectively). (1) Contrastive pitch accents (Mathiassen 1997:39; ̃/Ø = level, ^ = broken, ` = falling) … While stress is almost always on the first syllable, lexical tones are found on heavy syllables, i.e., syllables containing a long vowel, diphthong or a sonorant coda, anywhere in the word (Steinbergs 1977, see 2).
tone_statements.locator: p. 1, opening paragraph with ex. (1) and second paragraph before ex. (2). Poster panel 'The basic contrast': 'The central dialect (standard) has three tonemes: Falling, Level, Broken'.
tone_statements.summary: Three contrastive tones, level, falling and broken (stød-like), on heavy syllables anywhere in the word, one tone per mora; initial stress, secondary stress on heavy syllables; lexical H, L, Ø + H*.

tone_statements.citation: Hualde, José Ignacio & Tomas Riad. 2018. Interaction between word accent and intonational boundaries in Latvian. Proceedings of the 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 18-20 June 2018, 27-31. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAL.2018-6 (open PDF:https://www.isca-archive.org/tal_2018/hualde18b_tal.pdf)
tone_statements.quote: In standard Latvian, there is a lexical contrast between words with a level tone and words with a falling or non-level tone. We refer here to these tones as word accents. Surface word accent configurations are made up of both lexical and intonational tones. According to Kariņš [1], the falling accent is the marked member of a privative contrast. In this paper, however, we will remain agnostic regarding the precise nature of the contrast (privative, equipollent), but look for evidence in either direction. The lexical tone is associated with the syllable with word stress, almost always the initial syllable of the word.
tone_statements.summary: 2-way lexical tonal word accent (Level H* vs Falling/Broken H*L) on long stressed (initial) syllables; broken tone = optional glottalization in the standard, lexical in some dialects.

tone_statements.citation: Grigorjevs, Juris & Andris Remerts. 2004. Latviešu literārās valodas intonāciju funkcionalitāte mūsdienās [The functionality of the intonations of Standard Latvian today]. Baltu filoloģija XIII(2), 33-50. Rīga: LU Akadēmiskais apgāds.
tone_statements.quote: Trīs intonācijas (lauzto, krītošo un stiepto) šķir tikai triju intonāciju apgabalā … Latviešu literārās valodas triju intonāciju (lauztās, stieptās un krītošās) sistēmā ir iespējamas šādas intonāciju fonoloģiskās opozīcijas: 1) lauztās un krītošās intonācijas fonoloģiskā opozīcija; 2) lauztās un stieptās intonācijas fonoloģiskā opozīcija; 3) stieptās un krītošās intonācijas fonoloģiskā opozīcija.
tone_statements.translation: The three intonations (broken, falling and level) are distinguished only in the three-intonation area … In the three-intonation (broken, level and falling) system of Standard Latvian the following phonological oppositions of intonations are possible: 1) broken vs falling; 2) broken vs level; 3) level vs falling.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 44-45 and p. 46, section 'Rezultātu interpretācija'; cf. English Summary p. 50
tone_statements.summary: Three contrastive syllable intonations in Standard Latvian: broken, level (protracted), falling; young Low Latvian two-intonation-area speakers keep level vs non-level but barely broken vs falling.

tone_statements.quote: Historically, the third forte is a Latvian in.novation. It … appears on certain 1011g syllables; the domain of the tone is a long vowel; diphthong, .or sequence of vowel plus resonant, The third tone, whose phouetic nature is hinted at by its German names 11 Stosston'' or 11 gebrochene Intonation 1' , 3 contrasts in Latvian … . with the acute and circumflex tonesj the latter two will not be further treated in the -present article. Every long syllable has one of the three tonea.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 144-145 (introduction, running across the page break, with fn. 3 on p. 144 giving Ekblom's rising-falling + Stoss description); recapitulation of the acoustic finding p. 151.
tone_statements.summary: Every long syllable nucleus carries one of three contrasting tones: acute, circumflex, or the third (broken) tone, whose one constant acoustic cue is a mid-nucleus phonation break, not F0 direction.

sources.note: Primary stress is on the first syllable regardless of weight (undominated ALIGNHEAD + trochaic feet). Secondary stress exists (contra Halle & Vergnaud 1987 / Goldsmith 1990; supported by Karins' 1995-96 experimental work): short words (2-3 syll.) build moraic trochees L->R, long words (4-5 syll.) build syllabic trochees L->R, with some ternary and stem-stressed exceptions; all stress data taken from Endzelins 1922. Confirms fixed initial primary stress and adds the secondary-stress pattern (weight-sensitive in short words, alternating in long words).

sources.quote: 'In Latvian, stress generally falls on the initial syllable of the word. If the stressed syllable is heavy ... a three-way contrast in accent type in syllables is said to obtain.' Conclusion: 'Latvian having developed fixed initial stress, and Lithuanian retaining mobile stress.'

sources.note: Main word stress on the first syllable (citing Endzelins 1922); lexical tone (level/falling/broken) is independent of stress and occurs on all heavy syllables; primary stress is phonologically a H tone. Notes a lexical exception with non-initial primary stress: nekad 'never' stressed on the second syllable (ne- compounds), with pitch data from a Riga speaker. Confirms initial primary stress; refines by documenting a non-initial-stress lexeme.

The latter is comparable to Danish and Lithuanian stød (e.g., Basbøll 2005, Kiparsky 2015, respectively). (1) Contrastive pitch accents (Mathiassen 1997:39; ̃/Ø = level, ^ = broken, ` = falling) … While stress is almost always on the first syllable, lexical tones are found on heavy syllables, i.e., syllables containing a long vowel, diphthong or a sonorant coda, anywhere in the word (Steinbergs 1977, see 2).
sources.locator: p. 1, opening paragraph with ex. (1) and second paragraph before ex. (2). Poster panel 'The basic contrast': 'The central dialect (standard) has three tonemes: Falling, Level, Broken'.
sources.note: Three contrastive tones, level, falling and broken (stød-like), on heavy syllables anywhere in the word, one tone per mora; initial stress, secondary stress on heavy syllables; lexical H, L, Ø + H*.

Proceedings of the 6th International Symposium on Tonal Aspects of Languages (TAL 2018), Berlin, 18-20 June 2018, 27-31. ISCA. doi:10.21437/TAL.2018-6 (open PDF:https://www.isca-archive.org/tal_2018/hualde18b_tal.pdf)
sources.quote: In standard Latvian, there is a lexical contrast between words with a level tone and words with a falling or non-level tone. We refer here to these tones as word accents. Surface word accent configurations are made up of both lexical and intonational tones. According to Kariņš [1], the falling accent is the marked member of a privative contrast. In this paper, however, we will remain agnostic regarding the precise nature of the contrast (privative, equipollent), but look for evidence in either direction. The lexical tone is associated with the syllable with word stress, almost always the initial syllable of the word.
sources.note: Standard Latvian has a lexical contrast between a Level word accent (H* over the bimoraic nucleus) and a Falling/Broken accent (H*L); the tone is borne by the stressed (almost always initial) syllable and only when it is phonologically long (long V, diphthong, or short V + sonorant/x/v coda); the historical third 'broken' (glottalized) tone is lost as a lexical category in the standard, glottalization being an optional enhancement of the falling accent; some dialects instead keep glottalization and lose the tonal contrast. tone.translation: The article examines the role of the syllable intonation of heterotones in the perception and differentiation of word meaning. The relation of the three intonations of the standard language (level, falling and broken) to word meaning was studied in a perception experiment whose material consists of recordings of the pronunciation of the linguist Rasma Grīsle.
tone.summary: 3 syllable intonations (level, falling, broken) on long syllables in the standard norm; listeners from 2-intonation (level vs non-level) varieties merge falling and broken.
